items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' confirmation. 'But I can jump into all of that here with you and kind of get a good estimate for you' and 'we'll start with building up a profile for you real quick' are transitions, not a roadmap — the customer never heard what the call would cover or how long it would take, and never got to agree to it.

Access concerns were never probed at either end — no parking or truck-access question, no loading-dock or gate question, no COI, no elevator. This is a move inside a single apartment community from a second-floor unit to a townhome 'across the parking lot,' which means the entire job is walking distance and truck placement, and neither was established. He asked about narrow stairs and low ceilings but never about where the truck can sit at either door.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — not the name, not the $2,000, not repair/replace/reimburse, not the 60c/lb baseline. Zero insurance content on the entire call beyond the word 'insurance' inside the included-in-the-rate list. That is the differentiator most likely to survive a price comparison, and the customer is moving a gun safe.

Clock start was never stated. He covered the two-and-a-half hour minimum and the fifteen-minute proration cleanly, but never said the clock begins on-site when the contract is opened — so the customer does not know whether he is paying for drive time from the branch.

Truck count never stated. He said 'the smallest thing we can send to the team of two, that's the size team we would send for something like this,' which settles movers but leaves truck unaddressed on a two-bedroom-to-three-bedroom move.

Walk distance never asked or factored, and on this call that is the single largest variable in the estimate. The move is 'kind of across the parking lot' — there is no drive time, no stairs at the load-out beyond one flight, and no packing. How far the crew walks between two truck positions and two doors is essentially the whole job, and the estimate of three to four hours was built without it.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make the hours concrete.

Save Your Ass speech essentially absent. He gave the mechanic without the message: 'focusing on the large items, you're plan to have some of those other things either taken care of before or after the move' was stated as an input to the estimate, never as advice the customer could act on. Missing are the framing (prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill), the consolidation examples, the carload tip, and the sense-check. This was the most Save-Your-Ass-friendly call in the sample — the destination is across the parking lot from the origin, the customer is leaving town for a month and already boxing non-essentials, and he explicitly said 'the biggest thing is I just need help with the bigger stuff.' A carload speech here writes itself and was worth real hours.

No deposit required was never mentioned anywhere on the call. It closed anyway, so it cost nothing here — but it is the cheapest risk-reversal in the script and it went unsaid to a first-time customer booking a month out.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email. He described the notes ('I have included everything in my notes') without telling the customer the key details would be laid out at the top where they can be checked at a glance.

Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' The customer had two and had to volunteer both after Khevan had already closed — 'they don't have a problem taking a sectional couch part and moving that right?' and 'Do you guys do any kind of mill of veteran discount or anything like that?' Both landed after the sale was written, which means neither was used to build value.
No hours and no direct contact number given at the close.
Customer's name used twice ('Hey rich' and 'this is the best phone number to reach you out rich'), short of the 3-plus standard.

The military-discount question got a two-word answer — 'Unfortunately not.' — with nothing offered in its place. No value days, no acknowledgment, no thank-you for the service. The customer covered the awkwardness himself ('I'm just curious. Hey the dog, the dog border actually. Duke, oh, I was like, well you know, let me just ask'), which is the customer doing the rep's emotional work.
The one rapport opening on the call went unreturned. The customer offered a joke about his dog named Duke and got 'No, yeah, of course' — a filler acknowledgment, not a response.
top_strength: Khevan's discovery is the best in this week's sample, and his estimate is the one piece of estimate-accuracy behavior Amanda should actually hold up as the model. The probe was comprehensive and asked in the customer's language, not the form's: square footage, additional rooms ('a storage closet on a different level garage or anything like that'), specialty items qualified rather than just logged ('One gun safe' drew 'Do you know if it's over 500 pounds?' and then a real answer — 'it's like a five gun cabinet... almost like a filing cabinet type size'), packing needs, a box-count range anchored for him ('typically, we would see something in the range of 35 to 45 boxes for an apartment this size. Do you feel like, that's the range we might fall or would you have a bit more a fewer?'), additional stops, floors at both ends, the multi-level question on the townhome, special considerations ('are the, there's super narrow or steep or the ceilings low, anything like that'), and the stressor question verbatim ('Do you have any specific stresser or concerns about the moving process in general?'). He also knew which unknowns mattered and said so rather than burning time: when the customer offered to go look up the destination square footage, Khevan stopped him — 'it's not as important as the starting address especially if it's larger. Generally if it's smaller as where we start to consider additional time cause maybe everything doesn't fit, right?' That is a rep who understands why the field exists. Then the estimate. He stated the typical range honestly and then adjusted it downward, with his reasons on the record: 'Generally a two bedroom apartment. It's gonna take somewhere in the five to six hour range. Based on the fact that we're moving within the same community focusing on the large items, you're plan to have some of those other things either taken care of before or after the move. Then I would estimate somewhere in the three to four hour range.' Three specific job facts, each one a real reducer, producing a number below the typical band rather than above it — and then he covered the downside risk without padding: 'If we took an entire four hours, we're looking at $776. If we beat that estimate, there are no fees to make up the difference. Does that make sense?' He was also honest before he had to be, opening with 'with smaller moves or like with anything that's kinda low inventory or very small we may not be the most cost effective but we're happy to be, you know, service any move big or small.' That is credibility bought cheaply, at the top of the call, from a referral lead. The close is clean and the post-sale expectation-setting is the tidiest on the call: 'If you notice anything incorrect with the locations or the notes, then you can just let us know... We'll send you a meet your mover email a few days before you move. We'll reach out the day before to make sure there's no last minute changes and the guys will call you once they're headed your way.'
coaching_note: Start by telling Khevan what he did right, because it is the behavior the estimate-accuracy rock is built on. He is the only rep in this sample who stated a typical range and then moved the quote below it, with three named reasons on the record — same community, large items only, customer handling the rest. That is the discipline the bottom-four review is trying to teach, and it should be the example in the next calibration session. Now the fixes, in order. First, the biggest miss is not a script item, it is a job variable: this is a walk-distance move and walk distance was never asked. There is no drive, no elevator, and no packing — the entire clock is how far the crew walks from truck to door at each end and how close they can park at a townhome inside a busy complex on a Tuesday morning. Three to four hours could be right or could be two hours light depending on that answer, and nothing in the record tells us. Add one question: 'When they park, roughly how far is the walk to your door — and at the townhome, can the truck get close or is it a hike from the lot?' That question alone probably does more for the accuracy number on complex-to-complex moves than any rubric change. Second, this was the best Save-Your-Ass setup in the week and it scored a 2. The customer is leaving town for a month, already boxing non-essentials, moving across a parking lot, and told Khevan outright 'I just need help with the bigger stuff.' The speech: 'Rich, since you're literally going across the lot, here's how you cut this bill — anything that fits in a box or a bin, get it in one before we come, including the loose stuff in drawers and anything hanging on the walls. And anything small and awkward, run a carload or two over yourself in the days before. Every one of those is a trip our guys don't make, and on a job this short it adds up fast. Does that make sense?' Third, the differentiators are thin where the price comparison will happen. No Worries never came up at all, and this customer is moving a gun safe and a sectional — the two categories most likely to get damaged. Neither did the On-Time Guarantee. The full no-hidden-fees run was excellent and the inclusions list was complete, but a competitor can match a rate; they cannot match $2,000 of coverage with no deductible against a 60c-per-pound industry baseline. Fourth, warmth. The military-discount question deserved better than 'Unfortunately not.' Try: 'We don't have a formal one, unfortunately — but Tuesday the thirteenth is already our value rate, so you're on the best pricing we have. And thank you for asking, genuinely.' Same answer, no dead air, and it lands on the value day he already sold. Same with the dog joke, which was the customer reaching out and got a filler noise back. Use the man's name too — Khevan had it spelled out in the first minute and said 'rich' twice in twelve minutes. No estimate-accuracy concern to flag on this call; if anything, watch whether three to four hours holds, because if the walk turns out to be long this is the rare Einstein quote that is too low rather than too high, and that is worth knowing either way.
phone_presence_notes: Competent, efficient and easy to follow — 'easy enough,' 'no worries,' 'of course,' and real patience while the customer looked up dates twice — but the warmth stays transactional: the customer's name appears twice, the dog joke drew a filler 'No, yeah, of course,' and the veteran-discount question got a flat two-word 'Unfortunately not.' with nothing offered in its place, leaving the customer to smooth over his own question.
